lead: Abnormal combustion is any burning that does not follow the spark-plug flame front. The idea exists because normal SI combustion is a controlled flame sweep; when the end gas self-ignites or a hot spot fires early, the pressure rise becomes uncontrolled. You meet it in petrol engines during hard acceleration, low-octane fuel use, overheating or a Chennai summer traffic crawl. It causes the metallic ping called knock, power loss and, if repeated, piston damage.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for the three stages of SI combustion and Chapter 3.2 for flame speed and rate of pressure rise.

sections.h3: Normal flame travel and the end gas

blocks.text: In normal SI combustion the spark at the plug starts a small flame kernel. The flame front moves outward through the unburnt mixture. The mixture ahead of the flame is the end gas. It has not burnt yet.

As the flame grows, pressure and temperature rise in the cylinder. The end gas is compressed by the moving flame and by the rising piston. It gets hotter even before the flame reaches it. Designers keep this end gas below its autoignition temperature until the flame arrives.

Normal combustion is therefore a race. The flame must sweep the last pocket of end gas before that pocket ignites on its own. Flame speed and burn rate decide the race; see Chapter 3.2. If the flame wins, you get a smooth pressure curve with one peak near TDC.

Abnormal combustion is the case where something else wins. Two different events can make this happen. The end gas can self-ignite after the spark. Or a hot surface can ignite the mixture before the spark. The first is knock. The second is pre-ignition. Keep the order clear: the spark timing is the reference line.

Knock begins after the spark. The flame has already started from the plug. The end gas, the last unburnt part, reaches its autoignition temperature and burns very quickly. This self-ignition releases a local pressure pulse. The pulse reflects around the chamber and sets up pressure oscillations. You hear a metallic ping or pinking. On a pressure-crank angle trace, the normal smooth rise is followed by high-frequency wiggles. The crank angle at which those wiggles start is after the spark event.

Pre-ignition begins before the spark. A hot spot ignites the mixture early. The hot spot can be a glowing spark plug electrode, a carbon deposit, an exhaust valve edge or a sharp metal corner. Pre-ignition is not caused by the spark. It can start many degrees before the spark. It raises pressure and temperature early, which can then cause knock. The engine may run on after the ignition is switched off.

Detonation is severe knock. The end-gas autoignition is so fast that it sends pressure waves through the charge. These waves move at supersonic speed relative to the unburnt gas. They can reflect from the cylinder walls and piston crown. Detonation gives very high local pressures and temperatures. It can damage the piston crown, ring lands, head gasket and bearings. Some syllabi call ordinary knock 'detonation' loosely. In this book, use detonation only for the severe pressure-wave form of knock.
Visible symptoms are a metallic noise, vibration, loss of power and rising coolant temperature. Bad cases can end with a hole in the piston.

sections.h3: Reading the pressure trace and symptoms

blocks.text: To classify an event, mark the spark timing on the crank-angle axis. If pressure oscillations start after that mark, it is knock. If ignition starts before that mark, it is pre-ignition. Crank angles before top dead centre (bTDC) are negative in many data systems; compare numbers by time order, not by sign alone. Example: spark at 18° bTDC and event at 6° bTDC. 6° bTDC is later than 18° bTDC, so the event is after spark. Spark at 18° bTDC and event at 22° bTDC: 22° bTDC is earlier, so the event is before spark.

Mild knock is common and tolerable for short periods. Heavy knock or repeated pre-ignition is not. Damage starts at the hottest, most highly stressed metal: exhaust valve, piston crown, top ring land, head gasket. Pre-ignition can melt the spark plug electrode and then the engine may misfire or stop. For factors that make knock worse, see Chapter 3.4. For chamber shapes that avoid hot spots, see Chapter 3.8. We leave knock sensors and ignition control to Unit 2, and emission effects to Unit 6.

examples.question: A petrol engine has spark at 18° bTDC. In case A, pressure oscillations begin at 6° bTDC. In case B, a hot spot ignites the mixture at 22° bTDC. In case C, the pressure wave after knock travels at supersonic speed. Identify each case. Also give the crank-angle interval between the spark and each event.
steps: Fix the spark timing: θ_spark = 18° bTDC. A larger bTDC number is earlier in the cycle.
Case A: θ_A = 6° bTDC. 6° bTDC is later than 18° bTDC by 18 − 6 = 12°. The event is after spark. Pressure oscillation after spark is knock.
Case B: θ_B = 22° bTDC. 22° bTDC is earlier than 18° bTDC by 22 − 18 = 4°. The event is before spark. Ignition before spark is pre-ignition.
Case C: supersonic pressure waves after knock are the severe form. Name it detonation.
examples.answer: Case A is knock with the oscillation 12° after spark; case B is pre-ignition with hot-spot ignition 4° before spark; case C is detonation.
examples.check:
spark_btc = 18
osc_btc = 6
hot_btc = 22
after_spark = spark_btc - osc_btc
before_spark = hot_btc - spark_btc
print(after_spark)
print(before_spark)

traps: Do not classify by TDC. A pressure oscillation at 6° bTDC can be after a spark at 18° bTDC, because 6° bTDC is later in the cycle. Compare event time with spark time.
Knock starts after spark. Pre-ignition starts before spark. A hot spot at 22° bTDC with spark at 18° bTDC is pre-ignition, not knock.
Detonation is severe knock, not a third independent everyday event. If a question asks for the severe pressure-wave form of knock, answer detonation.
Ordinary knock is not early ignition. The spark has already fired. The end gas self-ignites later. Pre-ignition can lead to knock, but the names stay separate.

quiz.a: Autoignition of the end gas after the spark, causing pressure oscillations.

quiz.q: Why does the end gas get hot before the flame reaches it?
quiz.a: The growing flame and rising piston compress it, so its pressure and temperature rise.

quiz.q: Spark at 20° bTDC. Pressure oscillations start at 8° bTDC. Classify and give the interval.
quiz.a: 8° bTDC is later than 20° bTDC by 20 − 8 = 12°. The event is after spark, so it is knock, 12° after spark.

quiz.q: An engine runs on after switch-off and later shows pressure oscillations after spark. Explain the sequence.
quiz.a: A hot spot causes pre-ignition and run-on before the spark. The early pressure and temperature rise heats the end gas, so knock can follow after the spark.
Severe knock in which end-gas autoignition sends supersonic pressure waves through the charge.

quiz.q: Give two possible hot spots for pre-ignition.
quiz.a: A glowing spark-plug electrode and a carbon deposit; an exhaust-valve edge is also possible.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines use a knock sensor, a piezoelectric accelerometer on the block, to retard spark when it hears the characteristic ringing. Research engines use in-cylinder pressure transducers and optical access to watch the end gas ignite. Newer low-temperature combustion modes try to avoid the sharp end-gas autoignition that makes knock. Search next for 'knock sensor signal processing', 'end-gas autoignition imaging' and 'cylinder pressure knock metric'. The same ideas return in Unit 6 advanced combustion and in engine calibration work.
